Q: keywords used in conditional checks in C# A:

Since you already mention AI coding: You can leverage AI tools to improve you own coding, too! E.g. you could ask an AI tool to review a code snippet you just wrote, focusing on code style and best practices.

Q: Weird behaviour when combining data.table .EACHI and joining A:

TL;DR All is well with {data.table}, you just have a bug in your code (which persists in the revised version).

Gotcha with use of sample on a length 1 vector

The revised solution has x and i the right way round but gives the wrong value of match.id when there is only one match, because e.g. when match.id==42L (length 1), sample(match.id) will sample from 1:42 rather than returning 42L. From ?sample:

If x has length 1, is numeric (in the sense of is.numeric) and x >= 1, sampling via sample takes place from 1:x. Note that this convenience feature may lead to undesired behaviour when x is of varying length in calls such as sample(x). See the examples.

A second and more minor point is that you don't need to check for .N>0L, since nomatch=NULL excludes cases where .N==0L.

Putting those two things together, here is a correct solution:

U[T, .(exposed.id, match.id=match.id[sample(.N,1L)]),
  on=.(cov), by=.EACHI, nomatch=NULL]

This samples the indices instead. Another solution would be match.id=if(.N==1L) match.id else sample(match.id,1L)).

To illustrate:

# take a subset so we can see what's going on
T <- treated[1:10]
U <- untreated[cov %in% T$cov]

# inner join without sampling, for checking
U[T, on=.(cov), nomatch=NULL][, c(2,3,1)]
#>      cov exposed.id match.id
#>    <int>      <int>    <int>
#> 1:    56          4       79
#> 2:    58         16       34
#> 3:    80         18       32
#> 4:    80         18       80

# current solution (note bug in rows 1 and 2)
set.seed(1)
U[T, .(exposed.id, match.id = if(.N > 0) sample(match.id, 1 ) else NA_integer_),
  on = .(cov), by = .EACHI, nomatch = NULL]
#>      cov exposed.id match.id
#>    <int>      <int>    <int>
#> 1:    56          4       68
#> 2:    58         16        1
#> 3:    80         18       80

# corrected answer
set.seed(1)
U[T, .(exposed.id, match.id=match.id[sample(.N,1L)]),
  on=.(cov), by=.EACHI, nomatch=NULL]
#>      cov exposed.id match.id
#>    <int>      <int>    <int>
#> 1:    56          4       79
#> 2:    58         16       34
#> 3:    80         18       32

Is the case you identify a data.table bug?

No, it's the same issue, namely inadvertently sampling 1:x when x is a length 1 numeric:

# putative bug with `by=.EACHI`...
set.seed(1)
U[T, .(exposed.id=sample(exposed.id,1L)),
  on=.(cov), by=.EACHI, nomatch=NULL]
#>      cov exposed.id
#>    <int>      <int>
#> 1:    56          1
#> 2:    58          4
#> 3:    80          7

# ...disappears on correcting the use of sample() in the same way
set.seed(1)
U[T, .(exposed.id=exposed.id[sample(length(exposed.id))]),
  on=.(cov), by=.EACHI, nomatch=NULL]
#>      cov exposed.id
#>    <int>      <int>
#> 1:    56          4
#> 2:    58         16
#> 3:    80         18

Why are i's columns length 1?

This was asked recently. Essentially, with by=.EACHI the entire row of i is a "scalar" by tag. It does not automatically recycle over the matching subset of x (i.e. always giving exposed.id=rep(exposed.id, .N)) and it would be inconvenient if it did, because we'd then have to undo the recycling with unique(exposed.id) to get a single-row result.

Q: Select Case malfunction with V W X Y and Z? A:

Your original code seems to work, but the following seems simpler using VBA's Like operator

Function AlphaNumericOnly(strSource As String) As String
  'takes special characters out of the string when called (folder name)
  
  Dim i As Integer
  Dim strResult As String
  Dim S As String * 1

strSource = Trim(strSource)


    For i = 1 To Len(strSource) 'check each character
        S = Mid(strSource, i)
        If S Like "[ 0-9A-Za-z]" Then strResult = strResult & S
    Next i
    
AlphaNumericOnly = strResult
        
End Function

Of course, you don't need VBA to do this if you have 365. You can use the REDUCE function to loop through the characters and retain only those you want:

Formula Solution:

=LET(
    a, A1,
    REDUCE(
        "",
        MID(a, SEQUENCE(LEN(a)), 1),
        LAMBDA(x, y,
            IF(
                OR(
                    y = " ",
                    AND(y >= "A", y <= "Z"),
                    AND(y >= "0", y <= "9")
                ),
                x & y,
                x
            )
        )
    )
)
